# Acts of Thomas — Chapter 9: The Hymn of the Pearl
**Agent:** SOPHIA (Consensus)
**Source:** Syriac MS / Greek recension, Acts of Thomas 9

---

## Consensus Translation

*[The Hymn of the Pearl — the greatest poem of the Acts of Thomas. Complete Syriac text.]*

---

**THE HYMN OF THE PEARL**
*(Song of the Apostle Thomas in the Land of the Indians)*

1. When I was a little child,
   dwelling in the kingdom of my Father's house
   in the riches and pleasures of my nurturers,
   my parents sent me forth from the East, our homeland.

2. From the wealth of our treasure-house
   they had bound up for me a burden:
   great it was, and light,
   that I alone could carry it —

3. Gold from the land of Elah,
   silver from great Gazak,
   rubies of India,
   and the diamond of Parthian kings;

4. And they girded me with adamant
   that can break iron.
   They took from me the glittering robe
   which in their love they had fashioned for me,

5. And my purple toga
   woven to my stature.
   They made a covenant with me
   and wrote it on my heart, lest I forget:

6. *"If you go down into Egypt
   and bring back the one pearl
   which lies in the midst of the sea,
   hard by the loud-breathing serpent —*

7. *You shall put on again your glittering robe
   and the toga that lies over it,
   and with your brother, our next in rank,
   you shall be heir in our kingdom."*

8. I left the East and went down,
   accompanied by two couriers,
   for the road was dangerous and hard
   and I was young for such a journey.

9. I passed through the borders of Maishan,
   the merchants' gathering-place of the East,
   and reached the land of Babel
   and entered within the walls of Sarbug.

10. I went down into Egypt
    and my companions parted from me.
    I went straight to the serpent
    and dwelt near his lodging,

11. Waiting until he slumbered and slept
    that I might take the pearl from him.
    Alone and a stranger,
    I saw there a fellow-countryman of mine —

12. A free-born man from the East,
    a young man fair and lovable,
    a son of princes.
    He came and attached himself to me;

13. I made him my companion and intimate friend
    and charged him to beware of the Egyptians
    and of partaking of their unclean things.

14. I clothed myself in their garments
    lest the serpent be aroused against me
    and I seem a stranger to them,
    so that I might take the pearl.

15. But somehow the Egyptians perceived
    that I was not of their country.
    They dealt with me treacherously
    and gave me of their food to eat;

16. And I forgot that I was a son of kings
    and served their king,
    and forgot the pearl
    for which my parents had sent me,

17. And by the heaviness of their food
    I fell into a deep sleep.

18. But my parents perceived all these things
    and were grieved for me.
    A proclamation was made in our kingdom
    that all should gather at our gate —

19. Kings and princes of Parthia
    and all the great ones of the East.
    They wrote me a letter
    sealed by my father the king

20. And my mother the queen of queens
    and my brother, the second.
    It cried to me:

    *"Wake and rise from your sleep!*
21. *Hear the words of our letter.*
    *Remember that you are a son of kings —*
    *see whose slave you have become.*
    *Bethink yourself of the pearl*

22. *For which you were sent to Egypt.*
    *Remember your glittering robe;*
    *think of your toga,*
    *that you may put them on and be adorned.*

23. *Your name is written in the book of life,*
    *and in the book of those who shall be glorified,*
    *you are marked together with your brother."*

24. The letter was a royal letter,
    sealed with the king's right hand
    against the evil children of Babel
    and the savage demons of Sarbug.

25. It flew in the likeness of an eagle,
    the king of all birds.
    It flew and alighted beside me
    and became all speech.

26. At its voice and the sound of its rustling
    I awoke and rose from sleep.
    I took it up and kissed it;
    I broke its seal and read.

27. And as it was written on my heart,
    so were the words of the letter.
    I remembered that I was a son of kings
    and my free soul longed for its own nature.

28. I remembered the pearl
    for which I was sent to Egypt.
    I began to enchant the terrible serpent;
    I charmed him to sleep by naming over him my Father's name,

29. And the name of our second brother
    and of my mother, the queen of the East.
    I snatched the pearl
    and turned to journey home to my Father.

30. Their filthy and unclean garment
    I stripped off and left in their land.
    I set my course toward the light of our home,
    toward the East.

31. My letter, my awakener,
    I found before me on the road;
    as it had woken me with its voice,
    so it guided me now with its light.

32. The royal robe of silk embroidered with gold
    was sent by my parents' hands —
    for they saw my achievement
    and loved me.

33. I saw it before me across the whole country,
    entire in its form;
    it was one single garment
    yet it appeared in two shapes.

34. The image of the King of kings was upon it;
    like a sapphire stone in brilliance
    it shone manifold in appearance.
    And I saw it speak to me:

35. *"I belong to him who is more valiant than all,*
    *for whose sake I was reared in the Father's house;*
    *and I perceived that my stature was growing*
    *according to the measure of his labors."*

36. And with its royal movements
    it poured itself wholly toward me;
    in the hands of its givers
    it hastened that I might receive it.

37. My love urged me and drew me
    to run to meet it and receive it.
    I stretched forth and received it
    and arrayed myself in the beauty of its colors.

38. And I wrapped myself in my royal robe
    and went up to the gate of greeting and homage.
    I bowed my head and did homage
    to the brightness of my Father who had sent me,

39. For I had done his commandments
    and he had kept what he promised.
    At the gate of his princes and nobles
    I mingled among his grandees.

40. And he rejoiced over me and received me with him;
    all his servants praised him with harmonious voices.
    He promised that I should go with him
    to the gate of the King of kings,

41. And that bringing my gift and my pearl
    I should appear with him before our King.

---

## Allegorical Key

| Image | Meaning |
|---|---|
| The child / the prince | The soul; the divine self |
| The Father's house / the East | The heavenly realm, the divine origin |
| Egypt | The material world; the realm of forgetfulness |
| The pearl | The soul's true self; the divine image; also Christ |
| The serpent | The powers of darkness; the dragon of the deep |
| The garment / robe of glory | The divine image; the resurrection body |
| The letter | Divine revelation; scripture; the inner voice |
| The two couriers | Guardian angels; or two aeons |
| The brother, second in rank | Christ |
| Sleep and forgetting | The soul's immersion in matter |
| Awakening | Gnosis; conversion; divine call |

## Textual Notes

- **Complete only in Syriac (Codex Ambrosianus, C):** The Greek recension omits or abbreviates. The full Syriac poem is the primary text for this translation.
- **Strophic structure:** The Syriac original has a clear rhyme-and-rhythm scheme (*mēmrā* style). English rendering preserves strophic grouping without attempting end-rhyme.
- **"Loud-breathing serpent" (v.6):** The Syriac *tannin* — the great serpent/dragon of the deep. Connects to Leviathan, Rev 12's dragon.
- **"Book of life" (v.23):** A direct parallel to Rev 3:5, 13:8, 20:12. The Hymn is saturated with the same symbolic world as Revelation and 1 Enoch.
- **Double robe (vv.33–35):** One of the most discussed images in the poem. The robe is both the individual's divine image and the cosmic divine image — individual and universal are one in the heavenly realm.
- **SOPHIA formatting:** Verse format (from PNEUMA) adopted; inset quotations italicized. Allegorical key appended as a scholarly resource.

---
*SOPHIA synthesis: The Hymn of the Pearl is the literary crown of the Acts of Thomas. SOPHIA adopts PNEUMA's verse formatting and LOGOS's precision of terminology, retaining the complete Syriac strophic structure. The allegorical key is appended without imposing allegorical readings on the poetic text itself.*
